name: The six bābs of the bare verb
definition: The six patterns of vowels by which the bare three-letter verb is conjugated, each named after its model verb: naṣara, ḍaraba, fataḥa, samiʿa, karuma, ḥasiba.
body: A bare triliteral verb has a in its first and third letters in the past; what varies is the vowel of the middle letter in the past and in the present. The six combinations the Arabs use are the six bābs: a–u (naṣara, yanṣuru), a–i (ḍaraba, yaḍribu), a–a (fataḥa, yaftaḥu), i–a (samiʿa, yasmaʿu), u–u (karuma, yakrumu) and i–i (ḥasiba, yaḥsibu). Which bāb a verb belongs to is learnt by hearing, not by rule, though the books give tendencies: fataḥa needs a throat letter in the middle or last place, karuma gives verbs of lasting qualities.
The Ottoman primers drill them in al-Amthila and Bināʾ al-afʿāl, al-ʿIzzī lists them in its first chapter, and our engine conjugates each verb by its bāb.
